nodes.title: 1.2a-quick HS vs Uni (KKT): necessity + sufficiency
Applications
Application: Consumer Problem vs CE
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{APPLICATION: Consumer Problem vs CE --- same KKT recipe, different feasibility check.}}

\emph{Setup.}
\emph{(i)} \textbf{Consumer P} (one agent): $\max U(x)$ s.t.\ $p \cdot x \leq w$, $x \geq 0$.
\emph{(ii)} \textbf{CE} ($H$ agents with endowments $\omega^h$): find prices $\hat p$ and allocations $\{\hat x^h\}$ such that each agent maxes utility given $\hat p$, and markets clear.

\begin{tabular}{p{4.5cm}|p{18cm}|p{18cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consumer Problem (1 agent)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Competitive Equilibrium ($H$ agents)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1)} \emph{Write FOCs --- one per choice variable, for each agent.} \textcolor{orange}{Consumer P: $N$ FOCs total (1 agent). CE: $N \cdot H$ FOCs total ($H$ agents).} &
\textcolor{blue}{One agent, $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N$ FOCs}.

$\mathcal{L} = U(x) + \lambda\bigl[w - p \cdot x\bigr]$.
\[ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U(x^*)}{\partial x_i} = \lambda\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1,\ldots,N.\;} \]
\emph{$N$ equations, each pinning down one $x_i^*$.} &
\textcolor{blue}{$H$ agents, each with $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N \cdot H$ FOCs}.

Each agent $h = 1, \ldots, H$ solves \emph{their own} consumer problem with their own multiplier $\lambda^h$:
\[ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U^h(x^{h*})}{\partial x_i^h} = \lambda^h\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1, \ldots, N,\;\; \forall h = 1, \ldots, H.\;} \]
\emph{$N \cdot H$ equations: $N$ per agent, $H$ agents.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{(2)} \emph{Merge FOCs (take ratios) $\to$ optimality condition.} &
The famous optimality condition: Taking ratios of FOC$_i$ / FOC$_j$ eliminates $\lambda$:
$\underbrace{\dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}}_{\substack{\text{MRS}_{i,j} = \text{internal exchange rate}\\ = -\,\text{slope indiff.\ curve}\;(\dagger,\ddagger)}} = \underbrace{\dfrac{p_i}{p_j}}_{-\,\text{slope budget}}.$

{{img:0|w=380}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$N$-dimensional MRS.}} With $N$ goods, MRS is \emph{not} a single number --- it's a \textcolor{orange}{family of pairwise ratios}:
\[ \text{MRS}_{i,j} := \dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}, \quad \text{total of } \binom{N}{2} = \tfrac{N(N-1)}{2} \text{ pairs.} \]
Optimality: \emph{every} pair satisfies $\text{MRS}_{i,j} = p_i/p_j$. Equivalently, \textcolor{orange}{all $N$ ratios $MU_i / p_i$ are equal}, with common value $\lambda$ (the multiplier).
&
Same condition for each agent. Since the RHS is \emph{common} across agents (everyone faces the same prices):
\[ \boxed{\;\text{MRS}^1 = \text{MRS}^2 = \cdots = \text{MRS}^H = \tfrac{p_i}{p_j}.\;} \]
\textcolor{orange}{MRS equalization across all agents at CE.}
Within each agent, $MU_i/p_i$ converges to $\lambda^h$ (bang-for-buck equalized across goods). \textbf{Across} agents, $\lambda^1 \neq \lambda^2$ in general --- equal $\lambda$'s is a \emph{special} case (identical utility or same final bundle ratio, e.g.\ symmetric Cobb-Douglas).

{{img:2|w=680}}
This plot is the counterpart of the FOC optimality conditions: 1) the focs are a within agent condition; and 2) it is obvious the MU cannot easily 

\\
\hline
\textbf{(3)} \emph{Plug FOCs into BC $\to$ demand.} &
\]
\underline{Substitute} the FOC ratios into the BC $\Rightarrow$ each $x_i^*$ expressed in $(p, w)$ alone:
\[ \boxed{\;x_i^* = x_i^*(p, w)\;} \quad \text{(\textcolor{orange}{Marshallian demand}).} \]
\textcolor{orange}{Homogeneous of degree $0$:} $x^*(\alpha p, \alpha w) = x^*(p, w)$ for all $\alpha > 0$ --- scaling all prices and wealth leaves the budget set unchanged, so the optimum is unchanged. &
\emph{Same procedure for each agent}, but with each agent's \textcolor{blue}{own wealth} $w^h = p \cdot \omega^h$ (the value of their endowment at market prices). Result: \textcolor{orange}{individual Marshallian demands}
\[ \boxed{\;x^{h*}(p, \, p \cdot \omega^h),\;\; h = 1,\ldots,H.\;} \]
Each $x^{h*}$ inherits homogeneity of degree $0$: scaling $p$ scales $w^h$ too, so the demand is unchanged.
\\
\hline
\textbf{(4)} \emph{Feasibility check.} &
\textcolor{orange}{Embedded:} budget binds, nonneg auto from FOC. \emph{Nothing extra to check.} &
Each agent's budget is embedded. \emph{Two perspectives on aggregate feasibility} $\sum_h x_i^{h*} = \sum_h \omega_i^h$:

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{CE viewpoint (decentralized).}} Aggregate market clearing is \emph{not} a constraint in any agent's problem --- it must be \textcolor{orange}{checked separately}:
\[ \sum_h x_i^{h*}(\hat p,\, \hat p \cdot \omega^h) = \sum_h \omega_i^h \;\;\forall i. \]
These $N$ equations determine the equilibrium price vector $\hat p$.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Planner viewpoint (centralized).}} for the planner aggregate feasibility is \textcolor{orange}{embedded as a constraint from Step 1},\\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Footnotes on MRS interpretation.}}

$(\dagger)$ \emph{Internal exchange rate.} At what rate is the consumer willing to exchange $x_2$ for $x_1$? If $\text{MRS} = 4/2 = 2$, then $MU_{x_1}$ is twice $MU_{x_2}$, so the consumer is willing to give up \textbf{2 units of $x_2$ for 1 unit of $x_1$} $=$ \textcolor{orange}{internal price ratio}.

$(\ddagger)$ \emph{Slope of indifference curve.} Along $\{U = \bar U\}$: $dU = 0 \Rightarrow MU_{x_1}\, dx_1 + MU_{x_2}\, dx_2 = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\dfrac{MU_{x_1}}{MU_{x_2}} = -\text{MRS}.$

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Dynamics --- trade drives convergence (concrete numerical example).}}

\emph{Setup.} Consumer has $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2$: internally willing to give up \textcolor{blue}{$2$ units of $A$ for $1$ unit of $B$}. Market price: \textcolor{blue}{$1$ unit of $B$ costs $2.1$ units of $A$}, i.e.\ $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 1 (compare).} $\;\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2 \;<\; p_b/p_a = 2.1$. Market charges \textcolor{orange}{more for $B$} than consumer values it $\Rightarrow$ $B$ is \emph{overpriced} for this consumer.

\textbf{Step 2 (trade).} Consumer \textcolor{orange}{sells $B$, buys $A$}: pay $1$ unit of $B$, receive $2.1$ units of $A$ (better than internal rate of $2$).

\textbf{Step 3 (concavity of $U$ kicks in).}
$\bullet$ Less $B$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_B \uparrow$ (diminishing returns; see Plot 2).
$\bullet$ More $A$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_A \downarrow$.
$\bullet$ Hence $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = MU_B/MU_A$ \emph{rises} toward $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 4 (stop at tangency).} When $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2.1$: now to give up $1$ unit of $B$ the consumer demands $2.1$ units of $A$ in compensation --- exactly what the market pays. \emph{No further profitable trade $\Rightarrow$ optimum reached.}

\textcolor{orange}{In CE}: \emph{all $H$ agents trade simultaneously} until \emph{everyone's} MRS equals the common $p_b/p_a$. Each agent's individual MRS converges from their starting value (above or below $2.1$) to the common market value.

nodes.title: 2.1 Consumer problem: setup, v, x*, existence
2.2 KKT: FOCs + Walras's law
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.2 --- SOLVING via KKT: Lagrangian, FOCs, Walras's law.}}

\emph{Write budget canonically:} $w - \sum_n p_n x_n \geq 0$. \emph{Lagrangian (nonneg constraints absorbed into FOC slackness):}
\[ \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda) = U(x) + \lambda\bigl[w - \textstyle\sum_n p_n x_n\bigr]. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOCs.}} For each $n = 1, \ldots, N$:
\[ \tfrac{\partial U(x^*)}{\partial x_n} \leq \lambda^* p_n, \quad \text{with equality if } x_n^* > 0; \]
plus budget feasibility $w - \sum_n p_n x_n^* \geq 0$ and budget slackness: $\lambda^* > 0 \Rightarrow w = \sum_n p_n x_n^*$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Walras's law.}} If $\partial U/\partial x_n > 0$ for some $n$ (i.e.\ $U$ strictly increasing somewhere), the FOC forces $\lambda^* > 0$, hence the budget binds:
\[ \boxed{\;\textstyle\sum_n p_n\, x_n^*(p,w) = w.\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why KKT applies (Slater).}} For $U$ concave \& differentiable, use Ch.1 Theorem 2 (concave + differentiable: FOC iff optimum). Slater interior point exists trivially: e.g.\ $\underline x_n = w/(2 p_n)$ has $\underline x > 0$ and $\sum p_n \underline x_n = N w/2 \cdot \tfrac{2}{Nw}$ — pick small enough to keep slack. So FOCs are \emph{necessary \& sufficient}.

nodes.title: 2.3 MRS = price ratio (geometric)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.3 --- MRS = price ratio (geometric reading at interior optimum).}}

\emph{Rearrange any two interior FOCs} ($x_i^*, x_j^* > 0$): both $\partial U/\partial x_n = \lambda^* p_n$, so
\[ \tfrac{\partial U/\partial x_j}{\partial U/\partial x_i} = \tfrac{p_j}{p_i}, \qquad MRS(x_j, x_i) := -\tfrac{\partial U/\partial x_j}{\partial U/\partial x_i} = -\tfrac{p_j}{p_i}. \]

\emph{Reading.} MRS$(x_j, x_i)$ = how much $x_i$ the consumer gives up for one extra unit of $x_j$ = slope of the indifference curve in $(x_i, x_j)$ space (recall Ch.1: $\nabla U \perp$ indifference curve).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this must hold at $x^*$ (1-line economic argument).}}

Suppose at $x'$: $MRS(x_1', x_2') < -p_1/p_2$, i.e.\ $\tfrac{\partial U/\partial x_1}{\partial U/\partial x_2} > p_1/p_2$. Consider the budget-feasible move ``$+1$ unit of $x_1$, $-p_1/p_2$ units of $x_2$'' (along budget line). Utility change:
\[ \Delta U = \tfrac{\partial U}{\partial x_1} - \tfrac{\partial U}{\partial x_2}\tfrac{p_1}{p_2} > 0. \]
A feasible improvement exists — contradicts optimality. \textcolor{orange}{At $x^*$, no budget-feasible perturbation improves $U$.} Graphically: $\nabla U(x^*)$ (blue, $\perp$ indifference curve) is parallel to $p$ (red, $\perp$ budget line) iff the two curves are tangent.

nodes.title: 2.4 Duality + Slutsky equation
2.5 Demand elasticity
2.6 Indirect utility + Roy's identity
2.7 Equivalent variation + welfare
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.7 --- EQUIVALENT VARIATION \& welfare measurement.}}

\emph{Problem.} Utility unobservable. Trick: measure how a price/policy change \emph{compares} to a money transfer that induces the same utility shift.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Equivalent variation (with real endowments $\omega^i$, individual $i$).}} Using Roy's identity:
\[ EV_n^i = \dfrac{dv^i/dp_n}{dv^i/dw} = \omega_n^i - x_n^i, \]
where $\omega_n^i - x_n^i$ is the \emph{net consumption} (sign of net position determines who gains/loses).

\emph{Aggregate over goods and individuals.} Total welfare effect of a price change $dp$:
\[ EV(dp) = \sum_i \sum_n EV_n^i\, dp_n. \]

\textcolor{orange}{Applications:} tax incidence (a tax is a wedge in $p$); GE effects of reforms travel through equilibrium price changes; distributional analysis (sum $EV^i$ weighted by social weights).

nodes.title: 2.8 Homothetic preferences
2.9 Quasilinear preferences
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.9 --- QUASILINEAR PREFERENCES: no wealth effect on non-numeraire goods.}}

\emph{Setup.} Take good 1 as numeraire ($p_1 = 1$, $x_1$ unrestricted in sign). Quasilinear utility:
\[ U(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = \alpha\, x_1 + u(x_2, \ldots, x_N), \quad \alpha > 0. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consequence: $\lambda^* = \alpha$ regardless of $w$.}} \emph{Check from FOCs:} $\partial U/\partial x_1 = \alpha = \lambda^* \cdot 1 \Rightarrow \lambda^* = \alpha$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Demand and indirect utility.}}
$\bullet$ For $i = 2, \ldots, N$: FOCs $\partial u/\partial x_i = \alpha\, p_i$ depend only on $p$, \emph{not} on $w$. So $x_i^*(p, w) = x_i^*(p)$.
$\bullet$ All wealth effects fall on the numeraire $x_1^*(p, w) = w - \sum_{i \geq 2} p_i x_i^*(p)$.
$\bullet$ Indirect utility:
\[ v(p, w) = u(x_2^*(p), \ldots, x_N^*(p)) + \alpha\bigl[w - \textstyle\sum_{i\geq 2} p_i x_i^*(p)\bigr] = g(p) + \alpha w, \]
where $g(p) := u(\cdot) - \alpha \sum_{i\geq 2} p_i x_i^*(p)$.

\textcolor{orange}{Why useful.} ``No income effects'' means consumer-surplus measurements are exact ($EV = CS$); efficient allocations are independent of distribution of $x_1$ — standard in mechanism design / public economics.

nodes.title: 2.10 Labor supply: Frisch, comp., uncomp.
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.10 --- LABOR SUPPLY: uncompensated vs compensated vs Frisch elasticity.}}

\emph{Setup.} $c$ = consumption (numeraire), $h$ = labor (a ``bad''), $\omega > 0$ wage, $I$ = non-labor income:
\[ \max_{c, h\geq 0}\; U(c, h) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad c = \omega h + I. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Parametric: $\;U(c, h) = c - \dfrac{h^{1+1/\epsilon}}{1+1/\epsilon},\; \epsilon > 0.$}}

FOCs: $h^{*\,1/\epsilon} = \lambda^* \omega$ and $\lambda^* = 1$ (since $\partial U/\partial c = 1$). Plug in:
\[ \tfrac{1}{\epsilon}\ln h^* = \ln \omega \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \epsilon_{h, \omega} := \tfrac{\partial \ln h^*}{\partial \ln \omega} = \epsilon. \]
\textcolor{orange}{Constant labor supply elasticity} — and since $\lambda^*$ is constant in $(\omega, I)$, this equals the Frisch elasticity.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{General separable case $U = u(c) - v(h)$.}}
FOCs: $u'(c^*) = \lambda^*$, $\;v'(h^*) = \omega \lambda^*$.

\emph{Frisch (= $\lambda$-constant):} $\;\;\epsilon_{h,\omega}^F = \dfrac{v'(h^*)}{v''(h^*)\, h^*}$.

\emph{Uncompensated:} includes the income effect (which is $0$ iff $u(c) = c$). General formula:
\[ \tfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial I} = -\dfrac{\omega\, u''(c^*)}{\omega^2 u''(c^*) - v''(h^*)}. \]

\emph{Compensated (Slutsky):} $\epsilon^C = \epsilon - (\partial h^*/\partial I)\,\omega$. For separable case:
\[ \epsilon_{h,\omega}^C = \dfrac{u'(c^*)}{\omega^2 u''(c^*) - v''(h^*)}\,\dfrac{\omega}{h^*}. \]

\emph{Ordering (under standard signs):} \;$\epsilon^F \geq \epsilon^C \geq \epsilon^U$ (Frisch is largest because $\lambda$-constant means \emph{no} wealth-adjustment damping).

nodes.title: 2.11 Real endowments + chain rule
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.11 --- REAL ENDOWMENTS: $\hat x^*(p, \omega) = x^*(p,\, p \cdot \omega)$ and direct income effect.}}

\emph{Setup.} Consumer holds real endowment vector $\omega = (\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_N)$. Wealth $= p \cdot \omega = \sum_n p_n \omega_n$:
\[ \hat v(p, \omega) := \max_x U(x) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad x \geq 0,\;\; \sum_n p_n x_n \leq \sum_n p_n \omega_n. \]

\emph{Identity to nominal-wealth problem.} $\;\hat x_i^*(p, \omega) = x_i^*(p,\, p \cdot \omega).$ Net demand of good $i$: $\;x_i^* - \omega_i.$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Comparative statics --- chain rule with direct income effect.}}
\[ \dfrac{\partial \hat x_i^*}{\partial p_j} \;=\; \underbrace{\left.\dfrac{\partial x_i^*(p, p\cdot\omega)}{\partial p_j}\right|_{p\cdot \omega \text{ fixed}}}_{\text{usual price effect at fixed wealth}} \;+\; \underbrace{\dfrac{\partial x_i^*}{\partial w}\, \omega_j}_{\text{direct income effect via $\partial(p\cdot\omega)/\partial p_j = \omega_j$}}. \]

\emph{Checklist of inherited properties.}
$\bullet$ Existence: $U$ continuous $\Rightarrow$ $\hat x^*$ exists $\forall(p, \omega)$.
$\bullet$ Uniqueness/continuity: $U$ strictly concave \& continuous.
$\bullet$ Homogeneity degree 0 in prices only: $\hat x^*(\alpha p, \omega) = \hat x^*(p, \omega)$.
$\bullet$ Walras: $\sum_n p_n \hat x_n^* = \sum_n p_n \omega_n$ (if $U$ strictly increasing).
$\bullet$ $\hat v$ homog.\ degree 0 in $p$; increasing in $\omega$; \emph{not} always decreasing in $p$ (depends on net position).

nodes.title: 3.1 Exchange economy + Edgeworth box
3.2a CE definition + existence (sketch)
3.2b Walras's Law + GS uniqueness
3.2c Failures: nonmonotonic, nonconcave
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3.2c --- FAILURES OF CE EXISTENCE: nonmonotonicity \& nonconcavity.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Failure 1: non-monotonic preferences.}} Agent 1 strictly monotone, concave; Agent 2 only cares about good $h$ (flat indifference curves in $x_\ell$). Endowment: Agent 2 has \emph{all} of good $h$. Agent 1 indifference at $\omega$ has slope $0$ in $x_\ell$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Case (i): $p_\ell/p_h > 0$.} Agent 1 wants tangency point with $x^1_h > 0$; Agent 2 refuses to trade (would give up valuable $h$ for useless $\ell$). No clearing.
$\bullet$ \emph{Case (ii): $p_\ell/p_h = 0$.} Agent 1 demands infinite $x_\ell$ (cheap); infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Failure 2: non-concave preferences.}} Agent 2's indifference curves are not from a concave $U$ $\Rightarrow$ demand function is \emph{discontinuous}: small price change jumps optimum from a SE bundle to a NW bundle. Combined with Agent 1's perfect-complement preference (Leontief), no single price brings both demands to the same point.

\textcolor{orange}{Takeaway.} Existence theorem's hypotheses (continuity, strict monotonicity, strict concavity) are not just decorative — each rules out a real-world failure mode.

\emph{Exercise (worked example, Cobb-Douglas vs linear).} $U^1 = x^1_\ell x^1_h,\, U^2 = x^2_h$; $\omega^1 = (\omega_\ell, 0),\, \omega^2 = (0, \omega_h)$. CE exists? \textcolor{orange}{(Hint: Cobb-Douglas-style demand of agent 1 + agent 2's binary demand for $h$ alone — check market clearing of good $\ell$.)}

nodes.title: 3.3 Pareto optimality + Contract curve
3.4 Linear SWF ⇔ Pareto (Prop 6)
3.5 First Welfare Theorem (FWT)
3.6 Second Welfare Theorem (SWT)
3.7 Negishi–Mantel: prices = multipliers
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3.7 --- SOCIAL WELFARE via KKT: multipliers as prices (Negishi-Mantel).}}

\emph{Setup.} Max linear SWF with $\lambda \in (0,1)$:
\[ \max_{(x^1, x^2)} \lambda U^1(x^1) + (1-\lambda) U^2(x^2) \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; x^1_n + x^2_n \leq \omega_n,\; x^i_n \geq 0. \]
FOCs (with resource multipliers $\mu_n \geq 0$):
\[ \lambda \tfrac{\partial U^1(\bar x^1)}{\partial x^1_n} \leq \mu_n \;\;(=\text{ if } x^1_n > 0), \qquad (1-\lambda)\tfrac{\partial U^2(\bar x^2)}{\partial x^2_n} \leq \mu_n \;\;(=\text{ if } x^2_n > 0). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Negishi insight.}} By SWT, take $\hat p_n = \mu_n$: the social marginal value of good $n$ equals the equilibrium price. $1/\lambda$ and $1/(1-\lambda)$ are the marginal utilities of wealth at the supporting CE for the two consumers.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Connection to FWT.}} Price-takers in a CE choose PO because they face relative prices that equal the social planner's relative valuations — so individuals make the ``right'' marginal trade-offs.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Mantel algorithm (for CE computation via FWT).}}
1. Parameterize PO by $\lambda$ $\to$ get $\bar x(\lambda)$ and prices $p_n(\lambda) = \mu_n(\lambda)$.
2. Compute budget deviations $s^i(\lambda) := p(\lambda) \cdot (\omega^i - \bar x^i(\lambda))$.
3. Find $\lambda^*$ such that $s^i(\lambda^*) = 0\,\forall i$. With 2 agents: only need $s^1(\lambda^*) = 0$ (Walras).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Edgeworth example: Cobb-Douglas log utility.}} $U(x_\ell, x_h) = \alpha \ln x_\ell + (1-\alpha) \ln x_h$, $\omega^1 = (\omega_\ell, 0)$, $\omega^2 = (0, \omega_h)$.

\emph{FOCs $\Rightarrow$ prices and allocations:}
\[ p_\ell = \tfrac{\alpha}{\omega_\ell},\;\; p_h = \tfrac{1-\alpha}{\omega_h},\;\; x^1_\ell(\lambda) = \lambda \omega_\ell,\;\; x^1_h(\lambda) = \lambda \omega_h. \]
\emph{Budget deviation:} $s^1(\lambda) = p_\ell \omega_\ell - (p_\ell x^1_\ell + p_h x^1_h) = \alpha - \lambda$.
\emph{CE Pareto weight:} $\lambda^* = \alpha$. \emph{Relative price:} $\hat p_h / \hat p_\ell = \tfrac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\,\tfrac{\omega_\ell}{\omega_h}$ (depends on relative supply, as expected).

nodes.title: 4.1 Externalities: CE vs Planner FOCs
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.1 --- EXTERNALITIES: CE vs Planner mismatch (quasilinear endowment economy).}}

\emph{Setup.} Two agents, two goods. Quasilinear in numeraire $x$ (no externality on it):
\[ U^i(x^i, y^1, y^2) = u^i(y^1, y^2) + x^i, \quad i = 1, 2; \]
$u^i$ strictly concave, strictly increasing in own $y^i$. Prices $p_x = 1$, $p = p_y$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CE FOCs.}} Consumer $i$: $\lambda^i = 1$ (multiplier on budget), interior $y^i > 0$:
\[ \tfrac{\partial u^i(\hat y)}{\partial y^i} = \hat p \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tfrac{\partial u^1(\hat y)}{\partial y^1} = \tfrac{\partial u^2(\hat y)}{\partial y^2}. \tag{4.1} \]
Each agent only weighs his \emph{own} marginal benefit; cross-effects ignored.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Planner FOCs.}} Max $u^1 + x^1$ s.t.\ feasibility + $u^2 + x^2 \geq \bar U$. KKT $\Rightarrow$ $\mu_x = \lambda = 1$:
\[ \tfrac{\partial u^1(y^*)}{\partial y^i} + \tfrac{\partial u^2(y^*)}{\partial y^i} = \mu_y^* \geq 0, \quad i = 1, 2. \]
\textcolor{orange}{Social optimum equates the \emph{sum} of marginal utilities across agents} — externalities count!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Generic mismatch.}} $(4.1)$ uses private marginals; Pareto uses social marginals. They coincide only when cross-marginal terms vanish (= no externalities). \emph{Conclusion:} CE $\neq$ PO when externalities exist.

nodes.title: 4.2 One-sided externality: over-consumption
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.2 --- ONE-SIDED EXTERNALITY: agent 2 over-consumes, social optimum is not zero externality.}}

\emph{Negative one-sided externality.} $\partial u^2/\partial y^1 = 0,\;\partial u^1/\partial y^2 < 0$ (Agent 2's consumption of $y$ harms Agent 1; Agent 1's choice doesn't affect Agent 2).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{What happens.}} Social FOC:
\[ \tfrac{\partial u^1(y^*)}{\partial y^1} + \underbrace{\tfrac{\partial u^2(y^*)}{\partial y^1}}_{=0} \;=\; \underbrace{\tfrac{\partial u^1(y^*)}{\partial y^2}}_{<0} + \tfrac{\partial u^2(y^*)}{\partial y^2} \;<\; \tfrac{\partial u^2(y^*)}{\partial y^2}. \]
So $\partial u^1/\partial y^1 < \partial u^2/\partial y^2$ at $y^*$. By concavity + feasibility: \textcolor{orange}{agent 2 consumes \emph{too much} $y$ in CE relative to social optimum} (a feasible reallocation reducing $y^2$, raising $y^1$, Pareto-improves).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Social optimum is not ``zero externality''.}} The PO condition is ``sum of marginals = 0,'' i.e.\ Agent 1's marginal benefit from $y^1$ = Agent 2's marginal cost imposed on Agent 1. \emph{Some} externality is socially optimal.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two-sided negative externality \& destruction.}} If both $\partial u^1/\partial y^2 < 0$ and $\partial u^2/\partial y^1 < 0$ (passive smoking, etc.), at CE the sum of social marginals can go \emph{negative}: $\mu_y^* = 0$ in planner $\Rightarrow$ optimal allocation \emph{destroys} endowment of $y$. \emph{Example:} $u^i = \sqrt{x^i y^i} - y^{-i}$ with $\omega_y > \omega_x/4$ $\Rightarrow$ destruction.

nodes.title: 4.3 Pigouvian tax (internalize at margin)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.3 --- PIGOUVIAN TAX: internalize the externality at the margin.}}

\emph{Sharpened setup.} Only Agent 2 suffers; additive separable:
\[ U^1 = u^1(y^1) + x^1, \qquad U^2 = u^2(y^2) - \phi(y^1) + x^2, \]
with $u^i$ strictly concave/increasing; $\phi$ strictly convex/increasing (damage function).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Planner FOC.}} $\;\dfrac{du^1(y^{*1})}{dy^1} - \dfrac{d\phi(y^{*1})}{dy^1} = \dfrac{du^2(y^{*2})}{dy^2}.$ \emph{Agent 1's private benefit net of damage = Agent 2's private benefit.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Pigouvian tax mechanism.}}
Tax $\tau$ on Agent 1's $y^1$ consumption; tax revenues redistributed lump-sum $T^1 + T^2 = \tau y^{*1}$. Agent 1's problem:
\[ \max u^1(y^1) + x^1 \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; (p+\tau) y^1 + x^1 \leq p\omega^1_y + \omega^1_x + T^1, \]
FOC: $u^{1\prime}(y^1) = p^* + \tau$. Agent 2 untaxed: $u^{2\prime}(y^2) = p^*$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Optimal Pigouvian tax.}}
\[ \boxed{\;\tau^* = \dfrac{d\phi(y^{*1})}{dy^1} > 0.\;} \]
\emph{Reading:} the tax = \emph{marginal externality at the social optimum}. Forces Agent 1 to internalize the marginal cost imposed on Agent 2.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Equivalent subsidy formulation.}} Pay Agent 1 $s$ for each unit \emph{reduced} below $y^{*1}$: $s^* = -d\phi(y^{*1})/dy^1$ implements the same outcome.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Tax the externality, not its proxies.}} To reduce pollution from cars, tax \emph{pollution}, not cars. Otherwise distortion without internalization (e.g., firm switches to dirtier tech to cope with car-output tax).

nodes.title: 4.4 Coase + missing market
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.4 --- COASE \& MISSING MARKET: externalities $=$ missing market for externality rights.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Coase theorem (informal).}} If property rights over the externality are clearly assigned and bargaining is costless, parties negotiate to the Pareto-efficient outcome \emph{regardless of who holds the rights}. Initial allocation of rights affects only distribution, not efficiency.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Missing-market interpretation (Walrasian version).}}
Create a market for externality rights at price $r$. Suppose Agent 2 starts with rights to block $y^1$ entirely; sells $z^s$ units of right at price $r$.

\emph{Agent 2 (seller of rights):}
\[ \max u^2(y^2) - \phi(z^s) + x^2 \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; p y^2 + x^2 \leq p\omega^2_y + \omega^2_x + r z^s. \]
FOC: $\;\dfrac{d\phi(z^s)}{dz} = r$ \;(supply of rights, increasing in $r$).

\emph{Agent 1 (buyer):}
\[ \max u^1(y^1) + x^1 \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; p y^1 + r z^d + x^1 \leq p\omega^1_y + \omega^1_x,\;\; y^1 \leq z^d. \]
FOC (interior): $u^{1\prime}(z^d) = p + r$ \;(demand for rights = good price + rights price).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Market clearing $z^s = z^d \equiv \hat y^1$.}} Equate FOCs:
\[ \boxed{\;\dfrac{du^1(\hat y^1)}{dy^1} = \dfrac{du^2(\hat y^2)}{dy^2} + \dfrac{d\phi(\hat y^1)}{dy^1}.\;} \]
This is exactly the Pareto optimality condition. \emph{Creating the missing market} restores efficiency.

\emph{Real-world:} EU ETS (cap-and-trade for emissions, 2005-, with allowance auctions); tradable pollution permits in general. Limitation: works when there are many traders (price-taking is plausible).

nodes.title: 4.5 Public goods: Samuelson + free-riding
4.6 Pigouvian subsidy + Lindahl equilibrium
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.6 --- SOLUTIONS to public-good free-riding: Pigouvian subsidy \& Lindahl equilibrium.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Pigouvian subsidy (Groves-Clark flavor).}} Per-unit subsidy to consumer $i$: $s^i = u^{-i\prime}(y^*)$ (the marginal benefit to \emph{the other}). Agent $i$ then sees effective price $p - s^i$ and FOC:
\[ u^{i\prime}(y) = p - s^i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{summing}\;\;u^{1\prime} + u^{2\prime} = 2p - (s^1 + s^2). \]
With market clearing $c'(y) = p$: substitute $\Rightarrow$ Samuelson condition satisfied at $y = y^*$. \emph{Cost:} subsidies are large since you pay each agent the marginal value of \emph{all others}.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lindahl equilibrium (market-based).}}

\emph{Idea.} Unbundle the public good into $I$ personalized private goods: ``agent $i$'s enjoyment of $y$.'' Each agent has own price $p^i$; agent $i$ must buy the \emph{whole} amount of $y$. Single quantity, personalized prices — \textcolor{orange}{role reversal vs.\ CE} (where quantities are personalized and price is common).

\emph{Consumer FOC:} $\;p^i = u^{i\prime}(y).$

\emph{Firm} produces multiple ``copies'' of $y$ in fixed proportion (one per consumer), maximizes $\pi = \max_y (p^1 + p^2) y - c(y)$. FOC: $p^1 + p^2 = c'(y)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lindahl efficiency.}} Combine the two FOCs:
\[ c'(y) = p^1 + p^2 = u^{1\prime}(y) + u^{2\prime}(y), \]
\emph{exactly Samuelson} $\Rightarrow$ Lindahl implements $y^*$.

\emph{Limitation.} ``Each consumer is a price-taker in a market where he is the sole trader'' — informationally decentralized but unrealistic to assume price-taking with just one trader per market.

nodes.title: 5.1 States, contingent commodities, EU, risk aversion
5.2 Arrow-Debreu equilibrium
5.3 No agg risk + common priors → full insurance
5.4 Aggregate risk → prices favor scarce states
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5.4 --- AGGREGATE RISK: prices over-weight scarce states.}}

\emph{Setup.} Same as 5.3 but now $\omega_h > \omega_\ell$ (or vice versa) — aggregate quantity varies across states.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Result.}} Even with common priors, PO/AD allocations are \emph{not} on the 45° line. Both agents consume more in the abundant state: $\hat x^i_h > \hat x^i_\ell$ for each $i$.

\emph{Argument.} Suppose $\hat x^1_h \leq \hat x^1_\ell$. By feasibility ($\omega_h > \omega_\ell$): $\hat x^2_h > \hat x^2_\ell$. Then $|MRS^1| < |MRS^2|$, contradicting tangency.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Price ratio.}} Interior FOC:
\[ \dfrac{\hat p_\ell}{\hat p_h} = \dfrac{\pi_\ell\, u'(\hat x^i_\ell)}{\pi_h\, u'(\hat x^i_h)} \;>\; \dfrac{\pi_\ell}{\pi_h}, \]
since $\hat x^i_h > \hat x^i_\ell$ + concavity ($u'$ decreasing) $\Rightarrow$ $u'(\hat x^i_\ell) > u'(\hat x^i_h)$.

\textcolor{orange}{The price of contingent consumption is higher in the state where the good is scarcer} (relative to probability). This is the foundation of asset pricing: insurance-like claims (paying in bad states) are expensive.

nodes.title: 5.5 Time + assets: examples
5.6 Radner sequential equilibrium
5.7 SDF + master pricing formula
5.8 Complete markets: AD ⇔ Radner + Lucas tree
5.9 No-arbitrage, CAPM, risk-neutral pricing
6.1 Adverse selection: setup + First Best
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.1 --- ADVERSE SELECTION SETUP \& FIRST BEST (wine seller).}}

\emph{Buyer (Agent).} Type $\theta_i \in \{\theta_1, \theta_2\}$ with $0 < \theta_1 < \theta_2$ ($\theta_1$ frugal, $\theta_2$ sophisticated). Quasilinear utility:
\[ U_i = \theta_i\, q_i - t_i. \]
\emph{Seller (Principal).} Profit $\Pi = t - C(q)$, with $C$ twice diff, convex, $C(0) = C'(0) = 0$, $\lim_{q\to\infty} C'(q) = \infty$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First Best (type observable).}}
\[ \max_{q_i, t_i} t_i - C(q_i) \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; \theta_i q_i - t_i \geq 0 \quad (IR_i). \]

FOCs (binding IR + interior $q$):
\[ \boxed{\;C'(q_i^*) = \theta_i, \qquad t_i^* = \theta_i\, q_i^*\;} \]

\textcolor{orange}{Reading.} Production efficiency (MC = type's marginal value). Full surplus extraction (zero rent to agent). Indifference curves of agents are linear with slope $\theta_i$; iso-profits are $t = \bar\Pi + C(q)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why FB fails under hidden type.}} The sophisticated agent (steep indifference curve) gets strictly positive utility if he picks the bundle $(q_1^*, t_1^*)$ designed for the frugal. The Principal can't observe type to enforce assignment.

nodes.title: 6.2 IC, single-crossing, monotonicity
6.3 Second Best: NDT + downward distortion
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.3 --- SECOND BEST: which constraints bind, no distortion at top, downward distortion at bottom.}}

\emph{Problem.} $\pi$ = prob.\ of low type. $\max \pi[t_1 - C(q_1)] + (1-\pi)[t_2 - C(q_2)]$ s.t.\ $IR_1, IR_2, IC_1, IC_2$, $q_i \geq 0$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lemma (Binding constraints).}} At optimum:
\textbf{1.} $IR_2$ implied by $IR_1 + IC_2$ $\Rightarrow$ redundant.
\textbf{2.} $IR_1$ binds.
\textbf{3.} $IC_2$ binds.
\textbf{4.} With monotonicity $q_2 \geq q_1$ + $IC_2$ binding $\Rightarrow$ $IC_1$ redundant.

\emph{Why.} \textit{IR_1 binds:} else raise both $t$'s by $\epsilon$ (more profits, ICs unchanged). \textit{IC_2 binds:} else raise $t_2$ alone (more profits, IRs slack so OK).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Substitute the binding constraints into the objective.}}
$IR_1$ binding: $t_1 = \theta_1 q_1$. $IC_2$ binding: $t_2 = t_1 + \theta_2(q_2 - q_1) = \theta_1 q_1 + \theta_2(q_2 - q_1)$. Plug in $\Rightarrow$ \emph{relaxed problem in $(q_1, q_2)$ alone:}
\[ \max \pi[\theta_1 q_1 - C(q_1)] + (1-\pi)\bigl[\theta_1 q_1 + \theta_2(q_2 - q_1) - C(q_2)\bigr]. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOCs (interior $q_i > 0$).}}
\[ \boxed{\;C'(q_2^{SB}) = \theta_2\;} \quad \text{(\textcolor{orange}{no distortion at the top}),} \]
\[ \boxed{\;C'(q_1^{SB}) = \theta_1 - \tfrac{1-\pi}{\pi}(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\;} \quad \text{(\textcolor{orange}{downward distortion}).} \]
Convexity of $C \Rightarrow q_1^{SB} < q_1^{FB}$ and $q_2^{SB} > q_1^{SB}$ (monotonicity satisfied ex-post).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Information rents.}}
\[ U_2^{SB} = \theta_2 q_2^{SB} - t_2^{SB} = q_1^{SB}\,(\theta_2 - \theta_1) > 0, \quad U_1^{SB} = 0. \]
The high type earns rent $\propto (\theta_2 - \theta_1) q_1$. \emph{Trade-off:} reducing $q_1$ reduces the high type's rent but loses profit on the low type (proportional to $\pi$).

nodes.title: 6.4 General screening facts (any N types)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.4 --- GENERAL FACTS for the screening solution (with single-crossing, finite types).}}

\emph{Generic principles (extend to any finite $N$ of types under single-crossing, linearity in transfers, common outside option).}

$\bullet$ \textbf{No distortion at the top.} Highest type gets the efficient allocation: $C'(q_{N}^{SB}) = \theta_N$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Downward distortion below the top.} All types except the highest get a sub-efficient quantity: $q_i^{SB} < q_i^{FB}$ for $i < N$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Adjacent downward IC binds.} Each type $i > 1$ is indifferent between his bundle and that of type $i-1$: $\theta_i q_i^{SB} - t_i^{SB} = \theta_i q_{i-1}^{SB} - t_{i-1}^{SB}$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Increasing information rent.} Each type above the bottom enjoys $U_i^{SB} > 0$, and $U_i^{SB}$ is increasing in $i$ (more discrimination $\Rightarrow$ more rent for higher types).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Lowest type's surplus is zero.} $IR_1$ binds: $U_1^{SB} = 0$.

\textcolor{orange}{Intuition.} The single-crossing property allows the principal to use quality as a sorting device. The cost of sorting is the rent paid to high types to prevent them from mimicking; the benefit is being able to serve low types as well.

nodes.title: 6.5 Delegation: efficient type is low cost
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.5 --- DELEGATION VARIANT: efficient type is the \emph{low} cost; sign-flip of info rent.}}

\emph{Setup.} Principal delegates production. Output value $S(q)$ ($S' > 0$, $S'' < 0$, $S(0)=0$). Agent's cost type $\theta \in \{\underline\theta, \overline\theta\}$, $\underline\theta < \overline\theta$ — the \emph{low-$\theta$ is the efficient type}. Wage $t$.
\[ \Pi = S(q) - t, \qquad U(q, t; \theta) = t - \theta q. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First Best.}} $S'(q^{FB}_\theta) = \theta$; $t^{FB}_\theta = \theta q^{FB}_\theta$ (full rent extraction, $U = 0$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Second Best (interim IR).}} Now \emph{efficient} type $\underline\theta$ would lie down to get the inefficient contract (less work, same wage). Mirror-image of 6.3:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Binding constraints:} $\overline{IR}$ (inefficient indifferent to outside) and $\underline{IC}$ (efficient indifferent to mimicking inefficient).
$\bullet$ \textbf{Monotonicity:} $\underline q \geq \overline q$ (efficient produces more).
$\bullet$ \textbf{No distortion at the top:} $S'(\underline q^{SB}) = \underline\theta$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Downward (here: \emph{upward in cost}) distortion:} $\overline q^{SB} < \overline q^{FB}$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Info rent to the efficient type:} $U_{\underline\theta}^{SB} = (\overline\theta - \underline\theta)\, \overline q^{SB} > 0$; $U_{\overline\theta}^{SB} = 0$.

\textcolor{orange}{Symmetry.} The ``good'' type is the one with private information advantage that earns rent. In wine: high willingness-to-pay; here: low marginal cost. Single-crossing is symmetric to the role-reversal.

nodes.title: 6.6 Ex-ante: sell the firm restores FB
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.6 --- EX-ANTE CONTRACTING: ``sell the firm'' restores first best.}}

\emph{Timing change.} Agent commits to contract \emph{before} learning $\theta$ (vs.\ interim). One ex-ante IR:
\[ \nu[\underline t - \underline\theta \underline q] + (1-\nu)[\overline t - \overline\theta \overline q] \geq 0. \tag{$IR_0$} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Result: FB is implementable.}} Set
\[ \underline t^* = S(\underline q^*) - T^*, \qquad \overline t^* = S(\overline q^*) - T^*, \quad T^* := \mathbb{E}[\text{first-best profit}]. \]

\textcolor{orange}{Sell-the-firm interpretation.} Principal collects a fixed expected payment $T^*$; agent is residual claimant for the firm's profit in each state. As residual claimant, the agent internalizes incentives and produces efficient $q^*$.

\emph{IC check.} Concavity of $S$ + definition of $q^*$ at FB make both $IC$'s satisfied. \emph{Ex-post (interim) rents:}
\[ \underline U^* = (1-\nu)\bigl[S(\underline q^*) - \underline\theta \underline q^* - (S(\overline q^*) - \overline\theta \overline q^*)\bigr] > 0, \quad \overline U^* < 0. \]
Efficient type gets ex-post positive rent; inefficient gets ex-post negative — but \emph{ex-ante zero}, satisfying $IR_0$. The risk-neutral agent absorbs the type risk.

\textcolor{orange}{Takeaway.} Info rent disappears when ex-ante contracting is feasible \emph{and} agent is risk-neutral.

nodes.title: 6.7 Limited liability: 3 regimes by I
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.7 --- LIMITED LIABILITY on rents: three regimes by the floor $I$.}}

\emph{Setup.} Ex-ante IR + LL constraints: $\underline t - \underline\theta \underline q \geq -I$, $\overline t - \overline\theta \overline q \geq -I$ (ex-post utility floor).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Relevant constraints.}} $\underline{LL}$ is redundant given $\overline{LL} + \underline{IC}$ (since $\underline U \geq \overline U + \overline q\, \Delta\theta \geq -I + \overline q\,\Delta\theta \geq -I$). The relaxed problem keeps $\underline{IC}$, $IR$, $\overline{LL}$, monotonicity.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three regimes (with $\Delta\theta = \overline\theta - \underline\theta$).}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Regime (i): $I > \nu\, \overline q^{FB}\,\Delta\theta$.} Floor is so low it doesn't bind; only $IR$ binds. \textcolor{orange}{First best implementable} for both types: $\overline q = \overline q^{FB}$, $\underline q = \underline q^{FB}$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Regime (ii): $\nu\, \overline q^{SB}\,\Delta\theta \leq I < \nu\, \overline q^{FB}\,\Delta\theta$.} $\underline{IC}$, $IR$, $\overline{LL}$ all bind. Inefficient is distorted but \emph{less} than usual SB: $\overline q^{SB} < \overline q^L < \overline q^{FB}$. Efficient still at FB.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Regime (iii): $I \leq \nu\, \overline q^{SB}\,\Delta\theta$.} $\overline{LL}$ and $\underline{IC}$ bind; $IR$ \emph{slack}. Standard second-best quantities $\overline q^L = \overline q^{SB}$. Agent earns positive ex-ante rent: LL is too tight to extract everything.

\textcolor{orange}{Reading.} The looser the limited liability (large $I$), the closer to first best. Limited liability protects the agent against ex-post losses but lets the principal extract less rent.

\emph{Related: LL on transfers.} Constraint $\underline t, \overline t \geq -I$ leads instead to \textcolor{orange}{upward distortion of $\overline q$} and possibly \textcolor{orange}{bunching} (same $q$ to both types) when $I$ is very high.

nodes.title: 6.8 Monopoly insurance: high-risk full, low-risk partial
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6.8 --- INSURANCE under monopoly: high-risk gets full insurance, low-risk gets partial.}}

\emph{Setup.} Risk-averse agent, wealth $\omega$, damage $d$ with prob.\ $\theta \in \{\underline\theta, \overline\theta\}$, $\underline\theta < \overline\theta$. Bernoulli utility $u$ strict.\ concave, increasing. Without insurance: $U_0 = \theta u(\omega - d) + (1-\theta) u(\omega)$.

Contract $(t_a, t_n)$: $t_a$ = reimbursement (net of premium), $t_n$ = premium.
\[ U = \theta\, u(\omega - d + t_a) + (1-\theta)\, u(\omega - t_n). \]
Risk-neutral insurer's profit: $V = -\theta t_a + (1-\theta) t_n$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First Best (full insurance for both types).}}
Binding IRs $\Rightarrow$ FOCs give $\omega - d + t_a = \omega - t_n$, i.e.\ \textcolor{orange}{equal consumption in both states}. Risk fully eliminated.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Second Best.}} High-risk type $\overline\theta$ would mimic low-risk to grab more. Mirror of wine:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Binding constraints:} $\underline{IR}$ (low-risk gets exactly outside option) and $\overline{IC}$ (high-risk indifferent to mimicking).
$\bullet$ \textbf{No distortion at the top:} \textcolor{orange}{high-risk $\overline\theta$ gets \emph{full} insurance} (he's the ``high type'' in the sense that he values insurance more).
$\bullet$ \textbf{Distortion at the bottom:} low-risk gets \textcolor{orange}{partial insurance only} (lower coverage, lower premium) — used to discourage high-risk from mimicking.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Information rent:} high-risk earns positive rent; low-risk gets zero rent.

\textcolor{orange}{Real-world echo.} Health insurance ``bronze/silver/gold'' menus: high-risk (sicker) buy gold (full coverage); low-risk (healthier) buy bronze (partial). The screening sorts types via menu choice, and bronze underinsures relative to FB to keep gold expensive enough that healthy types don't migrate.

nodes.title: 7.1 MH basic + First Best (full insurance)
7.2 Second Best: IC + IR bind, wage gap
7.3 FB vs SB: when to implement effort
7.4 Continuum of actions: FOCA + likelihood ratio
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{7.4 --- CONTINUUM OF ACTIONS: First Order Approach (FOCA) + likelihood ratio.}}

\emph{Setup.} $a \geq 0$, $m$ outcomes with $p_j(a) > 0$. Contract $\mathcal{W} = \{w_j\}_{j=1}^m$.

\emph{Full IC is a continuum:} $\sum_j p_j(a) u(w_j) - a \geq \sum_j p_j(\hat a) u(w_j) - \hat a$ for all $\hat a \geq 0$ (intractable).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOCA: replace IC by the agent's FOC.}}
For interior $a^*$:
\[ \sum_{j=1}^m p_j'(a^*)\, u(w_j) = 1 \tag{agent's FOC} \]
\emph{Relaxed problem (double relaxed: write FOC with $\geq$):}
\[ \max_{(w_j)} \sum_j p_j(a)[x_j - w_j] \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_j p_j'(a) u(w_j) \geq 1\;\,(IC),\;\; \sum_j p_j(a) u(w_j) - a \geq \underline U\;\,(IR). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FOC of the principal w.r.t.\ $w_j$.}} With multipliers $\mu, \lambda$:
\[ \boxed{\;\dfrac{1}{u'(w_j)} = \lambda + \mu\, \dfrac{p_j'(a)}{p_j(a)}.\;} \tag{7.3} \]

\textcolor{orange}{Reading.} Both IC and IR bind ($\mu, \lambda > 0$); the wage in state $j$ moves with the \textbf{likelihood ratio} $p_j'(a)/p_j(a)$:
$\bullet$ High likelihood ratio (state $j$ becomes more likely as effort rises) $\Rightarrow$ higher wage $w_j$ (reward).
$\bullet$ Low/negative likelihood ratio $\Rightarrow$ lower wage (punishment).

\emph{Note.} The wage is \emph{not} indexed to output $x_j$ directly — only to the informativeness about effort. Optimal contract uses outcomes as signals of effort, not as a sharing rule.

nodes.title: 7.5 FOCA validity: MLRC + CDFC
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{7.5 --- FOCA validity: MLRC + CDFC sufficient.}}

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Proposition (FOCA validity).} If both conditions hold, the relaxed FOCA solution is incentive-compatible (i.e.\ agent's problem at relaxed contract is concave in $a$):

\textbf{(1) MLRC (Monotone Likelihood Ratio Condition).} $p_j'(a)/p_j(a)$ is increasing in $j$ for all $a$. Higher outcomes are ``more likely from higher effort.''

\textbf{(2) CDFC (Convexity of Distribution Function Condition).} For all $k < m$, $P_k(a) := \sum_{j \leq k} p_j(a)$ is convex in $a$. Marginal effort shifts distribution in a regular way.
\end{keydef}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Sketch of proof.}} Rewrite agent's objective via integration-by-parts:
\[ \sum_j p_j(a)\,u(w_j^R) - a = u(w_m^R) - \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} P_j(a)[u(w_{j+1}^R) - u(w_j^R)] - a. \]
Then:
$\bullet$ $u(w_m^R)$ constant.
$\bullet$ $-P_j(a)$ concave by CDFC.
$\bullet$ MLRC $\Rightarrow$ $w_{j+1}^R \geq w_j^R$ (from 7.3), so brackets $\geq 0$ — nonneg-weighted sum of concave is concave.
$\bullet$ $-a$ is linear (concave).
$\Rightarrow$ agent's problem in $a$ is concave $\Rightarrow$ FOC is sufficient. $\square$

\textcolor{orange}{Punchline.} MLRC $\Rightarrow$ \emph{monotone wage schedule} ($w_j^{SB}$ increasing in $j$). The relaxed solution is fully IC.

nodes.title: 7.6 Risk-neutral + LL: 3 regimes
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{7.6 --- RISK-NEUTRAL AGENT $+$ LIMITED LIABILITY: 3 regimes by floor $\underline w$.}}

\emph{Setup.} Agent risk-neutral: $U = w - a$. Floor $w_j \geq \underline w$ for all $j$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Principal's FOC.}} With multipliers $\mu$ (IC), $\lambda$ (IR), $\phi_j$ (LL):
\[ \mu\,\dfrac{p_j'(a)}{p_j(a)} + \lambda + \dfrac{\phi_j}{p_j(a)} = 1. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three regimes.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Regime (i): $\underline w$ low.} $\mu = \phi_j = 0$, $\lambda = 1$. Only IR binds. \textcolor{orange}{First best implementable}: ``sell the firm'' — $w_j = x_j - T$, $T$ chosen so IR binds. Effort: $\sum_j p_j'(a^*) x_j = 1$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Regime (ii): $\underline w$ intermediate.} LL binds for all $j$ except $j^* := \arg\max p_j'/p_j$. So $w_j = \underline w$ for $j \neq j^*$, while $w_{j^*} > \underline w$:
\[ w_{j^*} - \underline w = \dfrac{1}{p_{j^*}'(a^{SB})}. \]
Both IR and IC bind. Effort solves $\underline w + p_{j^*}/p_{j^*}' - a^{SB} = \underline U$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Regime (iii): $\underline w$ high.} IR slacks (LL prevents pushing utility below outside option). Principal extracts via the single ``bonus'' wage. Effort solves
\[ \sum_j p_j'(a^{SB})\, x_j = 1 - \dfrac{p_{j^*}(a^{SB}) p_{j^*}''(a^{SB})}{(p_{j^*}'(a^{SB}))^2}, \]
with $a^{SB} < a^*$ (under-effort because of LL-induced rent leakage).

\textcolor{orange}{Why reward at $j^* = \arg\max p_j'/p_j$?} The cost to relax IC per unit wage at state $j$ is $p_j(a)$, while the IC-tightening benefit is $p_j'(a)$. The principal pays only where the \emph{ratio} is best — i.e., at the most informative state about effort.

nodes.title: 7.7 Insurance MH monopoly (SB)
7.8 Perfect competition + credit rationing
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{7.8 --- PERFECT COMPETITION (insurance) \& CREDIT RATIONING.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Perfect competition under MH (Bertrand over utilities).}}

Two principals compete; agent chooses the contract giving higher utility. \emph{Symmetric Nash equilibrium:} both offer the contract that maximizes \emph{agent} utility subject to non-negative profits + IC + (binding) zero-profit constraint.
\[ U^M(\omega) := \max_{c_a, c_n} \pi(1) u(c_n) + (1-\pi(1)) u(c_a) - v \]
\[ \text{s.t.}\;\; [\pi(1) - \pi(0)][u(c_n) - u(c_a)] \geq v,\;\; \pi(1)(\omega - c_n) + (1-\pi(1))(\omega - d - c_a) \geq 0. \]

\textcolor{orange}{Role reversal vs.\ monopoly:} firm now has zero profit (IR for firm replaces firm's optimization). Agent gets max utility consistent with IC. Still partial insurance (IC binds).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Credit rationing under MH (2-project model).}}

$N$ firms, each chooses project $g$ or $b$: invest $I$, payoff $R_i$ w/prob $p_i$, $0$ w/prob $1-p_i$. $p_g R_g > p_b R_b > I$, $R_b > R_g$, $p_g > p_b$ ($g$ is socially better; $b$ pays more if it works). Risk-neutral, limited liability businessman.
\[ U_i(r) = p_i(R_i - r), \qquad \Pi_i(r) = p_i r - I. \]
\emph{Bank liquidity} $L$ with $I \leq L < NI$ — can't fund everyone.

\emph{IC for project $g$:} $p_g(R_g - r) \geq p_b(R_b - r) \Leftrightarrow r \leq \hat r := \tfrac{p_g R_g - p_b R_b}{p_g - p_b}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bank's optimal rate.}}
\[ r^{SB} = \begin{cases} \hat r & \text{if } p_g \hat r \geq p_b R_b \\ R_b & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

$\bullet$ Case $r = R_b$: firm switches to $b$, makes zero profit, no rationing.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Case $r = \hat r$:} firm chooses $g$, makes \emph{positive} profit $U_g(\hat r) > 0$. Yet bank \textcolor{orange}{voluntarily caps the rate} at $\hat r$ even though firms would pay more — raising $r$ would flip them to project $b$, lowering expected revenue ($p_b r < p_g r$).

\emph{This is credit rationing:} excess demand for credit at the going rate, but the bank doesn't raise the rate because doing so would worsen the borrower mix (the classic Stiglitz-Weiss insight).

nodes.title: 8.1 Spence model: pooling vs separating
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{8.1 --- SPENCE SIGNALING (simplified): pooling vs separating, single-crossing.}}

\emph{Setup.} Workers types $\theta \in \{\theta_\ell, \theta_h\}$ ($\theta_h > \theta_\ell > 0$). Fraction $\nu$ high. Education $e \in \{0, 1\}$. \textbf{Pure signaling}: education does \emph{not} raise productivity.

\emph{Wage = market expectation:} $w(e) = \mathbb{E}[\theta \mid e]$.
\emph{Worker payoff:} $U = w - v(e, \theta)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key assumption: $v$ decreasing in $\theta$ (single-crossing).}}
Education is less costly for high type. Standard form: $v(1, \theta) = 1/\theta$, $v(0, \theta) = 0$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Possible equilibria (simplified).}}
$\bullet$ \textbf{Pooling at $e=0$}: $w^*(0) = \mathbb{E}_\nu[\theta] = \nu\theta_h + (1-\nu)\theta_\ell$.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Pooling at $e=1$} (``rat race''): both go to college.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Separating}: $e^*(\theta_h) = 1, e^*(\theta_\ell) = 0$. Wages $w^*(0) = \theta_\ell, w^*(1) = \theta_h$.

\emph{Separating exists if} the high type prefers college: $\theta_h - v > \nu\theta_h + (1-\nu)\theta_\ell$, i.e.\ $(\theta_h - \theta_\ell)(1-\nu) > v$.

\textcolor{orange}{Reading.} Wages differ across pooling vs separating not because of fundamentals but because of \textbf{self-fulfilling market expectations} about workforce composition.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{10.2 --- TWO-PERIOD RECURSIVE SETUP + First Best.}}

\emph{Setup.} Two periods, iid shocks $\theta$ (period 1), $\theta'$ (period 2). Agent discount $\beta$; planner discount/bond price $q$. Continuation utility $w_n$ promised after period-1 shock $\theta_n$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Planner's recursive problem.}}
\[ \max_{\{\tau_n^1, w_n\}} \sum_n \pi_n[-\tau_n^1 + q V(w_n)] \]
\[ \text{s.t.}\;\; \sum_n \pi_n[u(\tau_n^1 + \theta_n) + \beta w_n] \geq U_0 \;(IR),\;\; \text{IC}(n, i)\;\forall n, i. \tag{10.3} \]

\emph{Sufficient statistic.} $w_n$ encodes the entire second-period continuation; static analysis (10.1) then determines $\tau_n^2$ to deliver $w_n$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First Best (shocks observable).}}
FOCs (without IC):
\[ w_n: -qV'(w_n^{FB}) = \beta\lambda, \qquad \tau_n^1: 1 = u'(\tau_n^{1\,FB} + \theta_n)\lambda. \]
$\Rightarrow$ \emph{full insurance:} $\tau_n^{1\,FB} + \theta_n = \bar c_1$ constant, and \emph{constant continuation:} $w_n^{FB} = \bar w$.

Rearrange (using $V'$ from 10.2): \textcolor{orange}{Euler equation for risk-free savings}
\[ \boxed{\;q\, u'(\bar c_1) = \beta\, \mathbb{E}[u'(c_2(\theta'))].\;} \tag{10.5} \]
\emph{Reading.} First best matches an agent with access to a risk-free bond at price $q$. No intertemporal distortion.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why FB fails under hidden info.}} At FB, each low-$\theta$ agent's indifference curve has steeper slope (single-crossing). \emph{All} agents would prefer to claim $\theta_1$ (highest transfer, same $\bar w$). FB violates IC.

nodes.title: 10.3 Second Best: LDIC binds, τ↓, w↑
10.4 Inverse Euler ⇒ positive capital tax
10.5 Hidden savings ⇒ bond economy (incomplete markets)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{10.5 --- ENDOGENIZING MARKET INCOMPLETENESS: SB collapses to a bond economy if agents can hide savings.}}

\emph{Setting.} Agents have hidden access to a risk-free bond at price $q$ (planner can't observe trades). Agent can adjust $(c_1, c_2)$ via the bond after receiving transfers.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consequence.}} Agent always declares the shock $\theta_n$ with the highest \emph{present value} of transfers $\tau_n^1 + q\tau_n^2$, then re-balances via the bond.

For IC to hold, the planner must offer a \emph{constant} present-value transfer:
\[ \tau_n^1 + q\tau_n^2 = \bar T \quad \forall n. \]

This means the planner can only implement the \textbf{static-equivalent} of an incomplete-markets bond economy: the agent gets a constant lump-sum and self-insures using the bond.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Result: micro-foundation of incomplete markets.}}
The constrained-efficient allocation with hidden savings = pure-bond-economy allocation (Bewley / Aiyagari / Huggett style: income risk + single risk-free asset for self-insurance).

\textcolor{orange}{Why this matters for macro.} A wide class of macro models — wealth inequality, business cycle costs, optimal monetary policy in HANK (Heterogeneous Agents New Keynesian) — assume incomplete markets exogenously. This dynamic-contracts result \emph{derives} that assumption from primitive private-information and unobservable-savings frictions.

\emph{Comparison summary.}
$\bullet$ Full information (FB): full insurance + Euler equality.
$\bullet$ Hidden $\theta$, observable savings: SB with positive capital tax (inverse Euler).
$\bullet$ Hidden $\theta$ + hidden savings: only bond-economy allocations implementable.
